Abstract A bank's reputation is a collective representation of the bank's image in the minds of the public or its stakeholders. Reputation reflects the public perception of a bank's actions; it can also be influenced by negative publicity about the bank. Reputation risk occurs because of other risks, such as credit, liquidity, and operational risks. This research utilizes quantitative secondary data from annual financial reports for the 2018-2023 period, obtained from the Bank Muamalat Sharia website. The data used in the study are documentary, specifically in annual reports published quarterly by Bank Muamalat Sharia from 2018 to 2023, and collected from the official website. This study was conducted at Bank Muamalat Sharia, examining the relationship between variables, including the influence of the distribution of Zakat funds (PDZ) and the use of benevolent funds (PDK) on the reputation of Bank Muamalat Sharia. The analysis was assisted by WarpPLS 7.0 software. Research Results reveal results. The distribution of Zakat funds has a negative and significant effect on Bank Muamalat's reputation, and the use of benevolent funds has a positive impact. Developing zakat and welfare funds is not just a moral imperative; it is a strategic move that can: Elevate transparency and ethical credibility, Drive financial performance and stakeholder trust, Align with maqashid sharia and bolster national and global Islamic finance standards, Differentiate Bank Muamalat as a trustworthy Islamic social intermediary. To solidify its identity as an ethical, socially driven Islamic bank, Muamalat must scale its welfare efforts and institutionalize transparency and inclusivity. Well-managed ZISWAF programs uplift communities and forge authentic trust and long-term social capital that will enrich the bank’s reputation well into the future. Research to date uncovers that while Bank Muamalat demonstrates some zakat infrastructure, the limitations in reporting transparency, narrow sample scopes, financial-centric measures, and internal- only perspectives obscure the actual reputational impact. Bank Muamalat is positioned to break new ground in Islamic banking by turning its existing Islamic value framing into structured zakat or welfare narratives in corporate reports. Pursuing societal-commitment metrics, building upon Malaysia’s benchmark success. Keywords: distribution of zakat funds, use of virtuous funds, bank reputation 1. Discussion This study's findings reveal important aspects of the relationship between the dimensions of benevolent funds and zakat funds, as well as the reputation of Bank Muamalat. First, PDZ has a significant and negative effect on reputation. PDZ (user of zakat funds) against Reputation results in an ineffectiveness path coefficient of -0.24 with a p-value of 0.12, greater than 0.05. This means it has a negative relationship with PDZ, increasing reputation by a contribution of 0.01, or approximately 1%. (Miranda & Fircarina, 2020) States that zakat does not affect reputation. This finding also aligns with research conducted (Suciarti & Wafiroh, 2023), which states that zakat does not affect one's reputation. Islamic banking requires Islamic banks to provide social services through qardh funds, zakat, and other donations, all by Sharia principles. Second, PDK has a significant and positive direct effect on Reputation. The figure yields a positive path coefficient of 0.68 with a p-value of 0.02, less than 0.05. It has a positive relationship with PDK in increasing reputation with a contribution of 0.47, or 47%. This is in line with research conducted by Muchlis and Utomo (2018), stating that Non-halal income, part of the benevolent fund, eroded customer trust after they became aware that non-halal funds are included, affecting the bank's reputation. This aligns with (Akbar et al., 2021) research, stating that benevolent funds affect bank reputation. Zakat management has a strategic role in strengthening the reputation of Islamic financial institutions such as Bank Muamalat. As one of Indonesia's first Islamic banks, Bank Muamalat must be committed to implementing Islamic principles, including social obligations through zakat. Zakat funds that are managed transparently and accountably will increase public trust (Bin-Nashwan et al., 2021). This trust is an important capital to attract and retain customers. Thus, a bank's reputation depends not only on its financial performance, but also on its social contribution (Doan et al., 2020; Esteban-Sanchez et al., 2017; Neville et al., 2005). The development of zakat funds and welfare programs does not solely function as a social activity, but also as an instrument of Islamic branding. A good reputation will provide a differential advantage in competition between Islamic banks. Bank Muamalat can use zakat funds to finance economic, educational, and public health empowerment programs. (Hoque et al., 2023). The real impact felt by the community will form a sustainable, positive image. This is in line with the purpose of maqāṣid al-sharī'ah, which emphasizes the welfare of the ummah (Firmansah et al., 2025). From an academic perspective, this research strengthens the literature on integrating Islamic philanthropy with corporate reputation. So far, reputation studies have focused more on profitability, service, and product innovation. However, https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Muhajirin et al. (2026) 9 little research links zakat management to the reputation of Islamic financial institutions. By examining the case of Bank Muamalat, this study provides an empirical picture that zakat can be an important variable in improving the image and credibility of the bank. This also opens up space for further research on the role of Islamic social funds in the financial sector (Ascarya, 2022). The practical implication of this study is the importance of Bank Muamalat to expand its zakat management strategy and welfare programs. This development is not only limited to conventional distribution, but also includes digital innovation , collaboration with social institutions, and measurable social impact monitoring. If managed professionally, zakat will be a strong reputation instrument while increasing customer loyalty. (Bin-Nashwan et al., 2021; Ma'ruf et al., 2025). However, strengthening zakat and welfare is not only a sharia obligation, but also a sustainable business strategy to maintain Bank Muamalat's position in the future. 6. Conclusions Per the research conducted, the aim is to see the effect of the Distribution of Zakat Funds and the Use of Policy Funds on the Reputation of Bank Muamalat in 201-2023, it can be concluded as follows: The distribution of Zakat Funds has a negative and significant effect on the reputation of Bank Muanalat, namely -0.24 with a p-value of 0.12 is greater than 0.05. This means that it has no relationship or influence on PDZ in improving Reputation, with a contribution of 0.01, equivalent to 1%. It shows that PDZ negatively and significantly impacts reputation, with an influence of 1%. Using Virtue Fund positively and significantly affects Bank Muamalat's reputation and the relationship between PDK and reputation. The figure yields a positive path coefficient of 0.68 with a p-value of 0.02, less than 0.05. It has a positive relationship with PDK in increasing reputation with a contribution of 0.47, or 47%. With a p-value of 0.02, PDK has a positive and significant effect on Reputation with an influence of 47%. The development of further research that reviews the impact of benevolent funds and zakat funds on the reputation of banks in the Indonesian Islamic banking sector. This research is expected to make a theoretical contribution to Islamic banking. As a suggestion for future research, it is advisable to consider broader variables, such as measuring the influence of technology and innovation on the management of benevolent funds and zakat funds, and their impact on the reputation of banks. 6.1. Future Research Directions Comparative Studies across Islamic Banks. The subsequent research can expand the scope of analysis by comparing the management of zakat and welfare programs at Bank Muamalat with other Islamic banks, both national and international. This comparison will provide a comparative perspective on the extent to which Islamic philanthropic practices contribute to the reputation and competitiveness of Islamic financial institutions—integration of Digital Platforms in Zakat Management. A study on fintech, mobile banking, and blockchain use in zakat distribution can reveal how digital innovation strengthens Bank Muamalat's reputation in the digital transformation era. JSON: Name: zakat_pdk_reputation_pipeline Title: Quantitative evaluation using panel causal inference and structural equation modeling of how zakat and benevolent fund allocations affect Bank Muamalat's reputation Short Hypothesis: An increase in the transparency-adjusted allocation of zakat and benevolent funds by Bank Muamalat causes an increase in the bank's reputation as measured by third-party deposit market share. Related Work: Existing studies analyze links between zakat/ICSR activities and Islamic bank reputation using firm-level financial disclosures, SEM/PLS techniques, and cross-sectional or short-panel samples. Methods typically rely on annual report variables (zakat amounts, benevolent funds) and reputation proxies such as deposit market share or stakeholder surveys. Reported results are inconsistent: some studies find positive effects, others null or negative relationships. Limitations across prior work include (1) reliance on single-bank or narrow-sample analyses limiting external validity, (2) use of financial-centr ic measures without independent transparency or stakeholder-perception metrics, (3) weak causal identification (correlational PLS/SEM only) leaving endogeneity and reverse causality unaddressed, (4) coarse temporal granularity (annual vs. quarterly) reducing power to detect dynamics, and (5) lack of ablation/robustness comparisons across modeling frameworks. These gaps motivate a longitudinal causal pipeline combining disclosure scoring, sentiment measures, panel causal models, and SEM for mechanism testing. Abstract: Problem: Prior work yields mixed evidence on whether zakat and benevolent fund management improves Islamic banks' reputations, often due to correlational designs, limited disclosure measures, and single-bank samples. Approach: This research builds a structured pipeline that integrates (1) quarterly financial and disclosure data from Bank Muamalat (2018–2023) and a multi-bank comparison panel, (2) a transparency/disclosure index for zakat/PDK reporting, and (3) stakeholder reputation proxies including third-party deposit market share and media sentiment. Analytical methods combine panel causal inference (fixed effects, instrumental variables, difference-in-differences or synthetic control where applicable) with confirmatory structural equation modeling to test direct and mediated effects. Contribution: The pipeline delivers causal estimates of the effect of transparency-adjusted zakat/PDK allocations on reputation, quantifies mediation by transparency and stakeholder sentiment, and provides ablation comparisons across modeling choices. Expected outcome: robust, generalizable evidence clarifying whether and how zakat/PDK allocation and disclosure practices causally influence Bank Muamalat's reputation and offering a replicable evaluation workflow for Islamic banks. Experiments: Datasets: (A) Bank Muamalat quarterly financials and annual reports 2018Q1–2023Q4 (n=24 quarters); (B) panel of peer Indonesian Islamic banks' quarterly financials and disclosures over same period (select top 8–12 banks by assets; expected panel N≈10 banks × 24 quarters = ~240 observations); (C) market-level third-party deposit (DPK) totals from regulator (OJK) quarterly; (D) disclosure documents coded into a transparency index (0–1) using a pre-specified rubric; (E) media and social-media corpora for sentiment scoring (national news outlets + Twitter) matched by quarter, producing a sentiment z-score. Variable construction: PDZ_qt = zakat_distributed / total_assets (quarter t); PDK_qt = benevolent_funds_used / total_assets; transparency_qt ∈ [0,1]; reputation1_qt = bank_DPK_share (%) ; reputation2_qt = media_sentiment_z. Baselines: (1) replication baseline: PLS-SEM model using PDZ and PDK -> reputation as originally reported; (2) pooled OLS; (3) bank fixed-effects (FE) panel regression with time fixed effects; (4) FE + instrumental variables (IV) where instrument candidates include exogenous zakat-regulation or national campaign indicators; (5) difference-in-differences (DiD) or synthetic control if a discrete policy/treatment event can be identified; (6) predictive baseline: regularized time-series model (ridge/LASSO) for reputation. Estimation details: estimate models with quarter and bank fixed effects, cluster-robust standard errors at bank level, include lags (t-1, t-4) for PDZ/PDK to test temporal effects. Evaluation metrics: coefficient sign and statistical significance (p-values), effect sizes (standardized betas), model fit (R-squared, adjusted R2), out-of-sample RMSE for one-quarter-ahead reputation prediction via rolling forecast (k-fold time-series CV), IV diagnostics (first-stage F-statistic), DiD parallel-trends test p-values, and placebo tests. Ablation studies: (A) full model (PDZ+PDK+transparency+sentiment) vs. (B) drop transparency variable, (C) drop sentiment variable, (D) PDZ/PDK only, (E) PLS-SEM vs FE panel — compare coefficient stability and predictive performance. Robustness checks: alternative normalization of PDZ/PDK (by deposits instead of assets), alternative sentiment models (rule-based vs transformer-based), and exclusion of quarters with missing or anomalous reporting. Required sample sizes and power: use the multi-bank panel to reach ≥200 observations for FE/IV power; report minimum detectable effect sizes given variance observed in preliminary data. Risk Factors and Limitations: Measurement error: PDZ and PDK amounts may be inconsistently reported across quarters or banks, causing attenuation bias. Disclosure coding: transparency index subjectivity and coder inconsistency can bias mediation estimates. Endogeneity and reverse causality: reputation may drive zakat/PDK allocations (reverse causality) and omitted confounders (marketing strategy, unobserved shocks) can bias causal claims; IV validity may be weak if no strong exogenous instruments exist. Sample size and statistical power: the single-bank quarterly series (n≈24) is small for time-series causal inference; multi-bank panel mitigates but cross-bank heterogeneity may limit comparability. External validity: findings on Bank Muamalat and Indonesian context may not generalize to other countries or regulatory regimes. Sentiment bias: media and social-media sentiment measures may reflect amplification or coordinated messaging and not unbiased stakeholder perception. Collinearity: PDZ, PDK, and transparency may be correlated, inflating variance and reducing power. Modeling limitations: SEM/PLS assumptions may conflict with panel causal models; inconsistent results across methods can complicate interpretation. Scalability and compute: media sentiment at scale requires substantial preprocessing but is manageable; however, extensive synthetic-control or IV searches increase analytic complexity.
